title: Blue Jays’ John Schneider irked with Yankees’ José Caballero’s pitch-clock antics
content:
TORONTO — The complete José Caballero experience was on full display Sunday.

Caballero played three different positions (second base, third base, left field), hit a three-run home run 420 feet to ice the game in the ninth inning and spent several minutes arguing with home plate umpire Steven Jaschinski, which earned him an “intentional delay” warning over the PA system.

Of all that, it was the intentional delay that irked Toronto Blue Jays manager John Schneider.

In the sixth inning of the New York Yankees’ 8-3 win, Jaschinski stopped the game when there were nine seconds left on the pitch clock and with Caballero in the batter’s box. Caballero was still looking at the dirt and lifted his head to acknowledge Blue Jays reliever Spencer Miles with eight seconds remaining.

By rule, batters must be in the box and alert to the pitcher by the eight-second mark or they’ll be charged with an automatic strike.

So Caballero did nothing wrong. That caused the Yankees’ utilityman to get in a prolonged argument with Jaschinski.

“There’s a lot of major league players in this league,” Schneider said. “There seems to be one guy that has an issue with it. It sucks that a pitcher like Spencer Miles has to sit out there for as long as he did. Seems like it could have been handled a lot quicker and a lot more efficiently than it was. But, again, that’s not why we lost, but it’s Major League Baseball, everyone knows the rules.”

Two innings later, Schneider was ejected after arguing a balk call on Blue Jays reliever Jeff Hoffman. Schneider said the umpires “could’ve put as much focus and attention on that play as they did the 10-minute conversation with José Caballero, who seems to have a problem with the pitch clock.”

This is not the first time this season that Caballero has argued with home plate umpires about the pitch clock rule.

He’s had several incidents arguing about opposing pitchers not acknowledging him before starting their windup, and several back-and-forth conversations with home plate umpires who are quick to warn him about acknowledging pitchers. It’s Caballero’s way of getting underneath his opponents’ skin.

“He was saying that if I looked down, he was going to call a strike on me,” Caballero said. “I don’t really understand the rule there. They’ve been changing the rules without any warnings. I don’t know why they’re doing that. The rules are the rules. Nobody wanted the rules. They invented the rules. They should take care of it. I’m just trying to play with the new system that they got us playing.

“It’s not like I invented the rules. I wish they were more clear with their rules. Obviously, they’re not. The only guys who can call whatever rules they invented is the umpires. If they don’t want to call it, why are we getting new rules every time?”

The rule was instituted in 2022 to help pace of play, though Caballero’s argument and Schneider’s ejection led to the opposite effect, as Sunday’s game lasted 3 hours and 14 minutes. Entering Sunday, the average 9-inning game was 2 hours and 41 minutes.

Yankees manager Aaron Boone said he will speak with MLB to get clarification on why Caballero was warned, considering he has the same routine every time he’s in the batter’s box, which is to acknowledge the pitcher at the eight-second mark, the last possible moment he is legally allowed to.

“I need it because I do the same thing over and over,” Caballero said. “I do the same move. It’s not my fault the pitchers rush a little bit. You can tell that every time the pitchers don’t rush, it’s no problem at all. But whenever they get (runners) on and they start thinking faster and they rush, that’s when the problem comes. But that’s not my fault. I do the same thing over and over, so please come out here and tell us the actual rule because I’m kind of confused at this point.”

Caballero said from that point on, he was not in his “happy zone.” He took out his anger with his homer off reliever Tommy Nance. That was the fourth-longest home run of Caballero’s career, and the second-slowest home run trot he’s had.

“I was enjoying it,” Caballero said with a wide grin on his face.

The win clinched the series for New York, marking the first time since 2023 that the Yankees have won a series at Rogers Centre. They did so without several key players, including Aaron Judge, Max Fried and Giancarlo Stanton. With the win, the Yankees remained in first in the AL East, while the Blue Jays dropped to 10 games back.

Since their first series against the Blue Jays earlier this season, several Yankees said that they felt like revenge was necessary after Toronto ended New York’s World Series hopes last year. So far, the Yankees lead the season series 4-3.

“We don’t like those guys over there, and they don’t like us,” Yankees starter Will Warren said.
